subsection: 1. The Home Rule movement: origins, Butt and the rise of Parnell, 1870–1885

notes.h: Isaac Butt and the Home Government Association (1870)
notes.b: Butt, a Dublin barrister and former Conservative MP, set up a moderate movement to win self-government for Ireland within the United Kingdom.
points: Isaac Butt (1813–1879) founded the Home Government Association in Dublin in 1870, bringing together Protestant and Catholic moderates, Liberals and former Repealers.
Butt’s aim was a federal settlement: an Irish parliament in Dublin for domestic affairs, while Westminster kept control of the empire, defence and foreign policy.
Butt rejected physical force and relied on constitutional methods: candidates, parliamentary motions and public meetings.
The Home Government Association was replaced by the Home Rule League in 1873, which was the organisation behind the first Home Rule MPs.
The secret ballot, introduced by the Ballot Act of 1872, reduced landlord and clergy pressure on voters and made the new movement’s electoral gains possible.
Butt had no formal means to discipline MPs, so a Home Rule member could vote or act against the party line without penalty.
The movement’s early funding and organisation were weak, and it struggled to turn sympathy among Catholics and Liberals into a unified national campaign.

notes.h: The 1874 election and the limits of Butt’s methods
notes.b: The 1874 election gave Home Rule a substantial bloc of MPs, but Butt’s methods won no legislation.
points: In the 1874 general election about 59 of the 103 Irish seats went to Home Rule candidates.
The Home Rule group in 1874 contained a mix of Catholic and Protestant MPs, and many were not bound to act together.
Butt used motions and debate rather than sustained pressure, and Westminster rejected Home Rule proposals in the 1870s.
By the late 1870s Butt’s leadership was challenged by younger MPs who wanted more aggressive parliamentary tactics.
Butt’s failure to win concessions left the party open to a new leader and new methods.

notes.b: Younger Home Rulers used obstruction to force Westminster to deal with Irish business, and Parnell learned the tactic from them.
points: Obstruction meant prolonged speeches, repeated amendments and objections that stopped Commons business until it was delayed or dropped.
Joseph Biggar, MP for Cavan, was the best-known obstructionist, and he worked alongside Parnell from 1877.
Obstruction showed that a small group of Irish MPs could disrupt the imperial parliament, which gave Home Rule a new kind of leverage.
The tactic was unpopular with many MPs and with the Liberal leadership, which saw it as a misuse of Commons time.
Parnell’s parliamentary tactics combined obstruction with the agitation that was spreading through the countryside after the agricultural depression began.

notes.b: An informal understanding between constitutional nationalists, Fenian-linked activists and land campaigners.
points: The New Departure brought together Michael Davitt, John Devoy of the Clan na Gael in the United States, and Parnell.
Its central idea was to link the land question with the Home Rule demand, so that tenant grievances would support a national movement.
Devoy and the Clan na Gael supplied American money and support for an agitation in Ireland, and Davitt organised the land meetings.
Davitt’s Mayo meetings at Irishtown in 1879 gave the New Departure its first public expression in the countryside.
The New Departure was not a formal agreement, and its leaders differed over whether the land struggle or Home Rule should come first.

notes.b: Parnell combined the Land League with the parliamentary party, and tied the two together through a national organisation.
points: The Irish National Land League was founded in Dublin in October 1879, and Parnell was elected its president.
In 1880 Parnell was chosen chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party, and he required candidates to pledge to act with the party.
The party took control of constituency selection through local conventions and the National League network, which replaced older local patronage.
The party’s newspaper, United Ireland, founded in 1881 and edited by William O’Brien, carried Parnell’s message to the country.
The Irish National League, founded in October 1882, succeeded the Land League and became the organising body for the Home Rule party.
Parnell was arrested in October 1881 under the Coercion Act and held in Kilmainham Gaol until May 1882.

notes.h: The Kilmainham Treaty and the Phoenix Park murders (1882)
notes.b: The Kilmainham arrangement between Parnell and Gladstone ended Parnell’s imprisonment, but a political murder followed within weeks.
points: The Kilmainham Treaty of April–May 1882 was an understanding between Parnell and Gladstone: Parnell was released, and the government agreed to ease the coercion and to pass a land measure.
The Arrears Act of 1882, which cleared part of the arrears of rent owed by tenants, was one of the concessions that followed the Kilmainham arrangement.
Unionists and Conservatives condemned the arrangement as a surrender to agitation, while radical critics in the League felt Parnell had traded away the land campaign.
On 6 May 1882 Lord Frederick Cavendish, the new Chief Secretary, and Thomas Henry Burke, the Under-Secretary, were murdered in Phoenix Park, Dublin.
The Phoenix Park murders were carried out by the Invincibles, a small group linked to the IRB, and their act was condemned by Parnell and by the nationalist press.
The murders strengthened the coercion lobby and made the government less willing to offer further concessions to the Irish party.

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Stewart Parnell (part 1: background and rise)
notes.b: Parnell’s rise rested on the combination of obstruction, land agitation and a disciplined party organisation.
points: Born in 1846 at Avondale, Co. Wicklow, into a Protestant landowning family, Parnell was a landlord’s son who made his name as a nationalist.
He was first elected MP for Meath in 1875, and he entered Parliament as a Home Ruler who wanted Irish self-government within the empire.
As a participant, Parnell led the Land League and the parliamentary party at the centre of the events described above, rather than observing them.
Supporters admired his cool, reserved manner and his discipline, and some called him the uncrowned king of Ireland.
Opponents in the press, including The Times, portrayed him as a sympathiser with violence, and unionists regarded him as a dangerous revolutionary.
Historians differ: some see his tactics as a realistic use of pressure to win concessions, while others stress his ambiguity towards agrarian violence and land agitation.

notes.h: Gladstone’s government and the Home Rule question (1880–1885)
notes.b: Gladstone’s second ministry combined coercion with reform, and its fall in 1885 gave Parnell’s party the chance to hold the balance of power.
points: Gladstone formed a Liberal government in April 1880, after the general election of that year.
Gladstone paired the Protection of Person and Property Act 1881, a coercion measure, with the Land Act of 1881 that set up land courts to fix fair rents.
Gladstone’s Liberal government was defeated in the Commons in June 1885 on a budget amendment, and Lord Salisbury’s Conservatives took office.
Salisbury’s minority government depended on the votes of the Irish party, and it used the Ashbourne Act of 1885 to fund tenant land purchase.
The Irish party’s decision to vote against the Liberals in June 1885 was the first clear demonstration of its power to bring down a British government.

notes.b: The two leaders differed in temperament, method and attitude to the land question, which shaped the movement after 1879.
points: Butt was a moderate who tried to persuade Westminster, while Parnell used pressure, obstruction and the threat of disruption to force concessions.
Butt accepted the Land Act of 1870 as a settlement of the land question, whereas Parnell made the land campaign the centre of the national movement.
Butt’s party had no effective discipline, while Parnell required pledges and used local conventions to control candidates.
Butt had little contact with the mass of tenants, whereas the Land League put Parnell in direct touch with the countryside.
Butt died in 1879, and the leadership passed to Parnell, who had already shown in obstruction and the Land League that he would use confrontation where Butt had used argument.

notes.h: Assessment: the early Home Rule movement
notes.b: Judgements on the 1870–1885 movement turn on whether its strength came from Butt’s constitutional approach or from Parnell’s organisation and tactics.
points: Butt’s achievement was to create a national party and place Home Rule on the agenda at Westminster; his limit was the lack of party discipline and the failure to win any concession.
Parnell’s achievement was to build a party able to hold the balance of power in the Commons by 1885; his limit was reliance on the land agitation, which he could not fully control.
Contemporary Liberals and Conservatives tended to see obstruction as an abuse of Parliament, while nationalists saw it as the only means to make Westminster listen.
Kilmainham was seen by contemporaries as a political deal, but later historians often treat it as the turning point towards a constitutional, land-reform strategy.
Butt is often judged as a moderate who opened the way, and Parnell as the leader who turned Home Rule into a national movement that Westminster could not ignore.

keyTerms.definition: The demand for an Irish parliament in Dublin to manage Irish domestic affairs, while Westminster kept imperial matters.
The moderate body founded by Isaac Butt in 1870 to campaign for Home Rule through constitutional means.
The organisation formed in 1873 to unite Home Rule MPs and supporters, succeeded by Parnell’s party machine.
Government through elected representatives, which in this period meant widening the franchise and protecting voters through the secret ballot.
Organised public pressure for political change, using meetings, newspapers, petitions, boycotts and parliamentary tactics.
A parliamentary tactic of prolonged speeches and amendments used to halt Commons business until the government yielded.
The 1878–79 understanding between constitutional nationalists, Fenian-linked activists and land campaigners to link Home Rule with land reform.
The 1882 understanding between Parnell and Gladstone that released Parnell and led to the Arrears Act and land measures.
The Home Rule group of Irish MPs at Westminster, which Parnell led from 1880 and bound by pledges to act together.
